claims.claim: Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate around AD 30.
claims.source: Tacitus, Annals 15.44; the four Gospels; standard scholarship.

claims.claim: Paul passed on 'that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures' (1 Corinthians 15:3), around AD 54.
claims.source: 1 Corinthians 15:3 (WEB); standard dating of 1 Corinthians.

claims.claim: Leviticus is credited by tradition to Moses; most scholars date its final form to the 500s–400s BC.
claims.source: Standard introductions; J. Milgrom, Leviticus 1–16 (1991).

claims.claim: Origen said of Hebrews 'who wrote it, God knows'.
claims.source: Eusebius, Church History VI.25.14.

claims.claim: The mercy seat (kapporet) shares a root with kippur; the Septuagint calls it hilasterion, the word in Romans 3:25.
claims.source: Exodus 25:17 LXX; Romans 3:25; standard lexica.

claims.claim: Tyndale coined 'scapegoat' in his 1530 Pentateuch.
claims.source: Oxford English Dictionary, 'scapegoat'.

claims.claim: 'Atonement' was formed from 'at one' in the early 1500s; Tyndale used it in Romans 5:11 (1526) and Leviticus (1530); the KJV kept it.
claims.source: Oxford English Dictionary, 'atonement'; Tyndale's 1526 NT and 1530 Pentateuch.

claims.claim: Jacob Milgrom argued that the sin offering purges the sanctuary of pollution.
claims.source: J. Milgrom, Leviticus 1–16, Anchor Bible (1991).

claims.claim: The Alexamenos graffito, c. AD 200, Palatine Hill, mocks a Christian worshipping a crucified donkey-headed figure.
claims.source: M. Hengel, Crucifixion (1977); standard references.

claims.claim: Yohanan ben Zakkai comforted a disciple after AD 70 with Hosea 6:6 and acts of loving-kindness.
claims.source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan A, chapter 4.

claims.claim: Yom Kippur atones for sins against God; sins against another only after reconciliation.
claims.source: Mishnah Yoma 8:9.

claims.claim: Hundreds of manumission inscriptions at Delphi record slaves 'sold' to Apollo, c. 200 BC–AD 100.
claims.source: A. Deissmann, Light from the Ancient East (1908); standard epigraphic surveys.

claims.claim: Origen said the ransom was paid to the devil.
claims.source: Origen, Commentary on Matthew XVI.8.

claims.claim: Gregory of Nyssa used the fish-hook image (Great Catechism 22–26, c. 385).
claims.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Great Catechism 22–26 (NPNF II.5); NPNF chapter analysis in the fetched file.

claims.claim: Augustine called the cross the devil's mousetrap in a sermon for Ascension.
claims.source: Augustine, Sermon 263.

claims.claim: Gregory the Great used the fish-hook image around 590.
claims.source: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job XXXIII.7.

claims.claim: Gregory of Nazianzus rejected payment to the devil or to the Father; Oration 45 preached c. 383–389 at Arianzus.
claims.source: Oration 45.22 (NPNF II.7) and its NPNF introduction (fetched file).

claims.claim: John of Damascus rejected a ransom to the devil.
claims.source: John of Damascus, Exposition of the Orthodox Faith III.27.

claims.claim: Anselm rejected the argument that God had to deal justly with the devil.
claims.source: Anselm, Why God Became Man I.7 (fetched file).

claims.claim: Joachim Jeremias argued that 'many' in Mark 10:45 is inclusive.
claims.source: J. Jeremias, The Eucharistic Words of Jesus (1955 English ed.); TDNT 'polloi'.

claims.claim: Athanasius born c. 296, bishop of Alexandria from 328, exiled five times; date of On the Incarnation c. 318 or c. 335 debated.
claims.source: Standard patristic handbooks; A. Robertson's NPNF introduction.

claims.claim: C. S. Lewis called On the Incarnation a masterpiece in his 1944 introduction.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, introduction to On the Incarnation, tr. a Religious of C.S.M.V. (1944).

claims.claim: 'He was made man that we might be made God' (On the Incarnation 54).
claims.source: Fetched file, Robertson translation.

claims.claim: Gustaf Aulén's Christus Victor (1930; English 1931) sorted views into classic, Latin and subjective.
claims.source: G. Aulén, Christus Victor, tr. A. G. Hebert (1931).

claims.claim: 'Descended into hell' appears in the creed of Aquileia as reported by Rufinus, c. 400.
claims.source: Rufinus, Commentary on the Apostles' Creed 18.

claims.claim: The Chora Church Anastasis fresco dates from c. 1315–1321.
claims.source: Standard art-historical sources on Kariye Camii.

claims.claim: Anselm: born Aosta 1033, Bec 1060, Archbishop 1093, finished Cur Deus Homo in 1098 in exile in southern Italy.
claims.source: R. W. Southern, Saint Anselm (1990).

claims.claim: Cur Deus Homo in the Open Court volume was translated by James Gardiner Vose (Bibliotheca Sacra 1854–55).
claims.source: Introduction in the fetched CCEL file.

claims.claim: 'You have not as yet estimated the great burden of sin' translates 'nondum considerasti quanti ponderis sit peccatum'.
claims.source: Cur Deus Homo I.21 (Latin text, Schmitt edition).

claims.claim: Abelard's Commentary on Romans (c. 1133–37) gives the moral-influence view at Romans 3:26; condemned at Sens 1141; died 1142 at Saint-Marcel near Chalon.
claims.source: Abelard, Commentary on Romans II; M. T. Clanchy, Abelard (1997).

claims.claim: Bernard attacked Abelard in Letter 190, c. 1140.
claims.source: Bernard of Clairvaux, Ep. 190.

claims.claim: Aquinas held that God could have forgiven without satisfaction, but the cross was most fitting, and satisfaction superabundant.
claims.source: Summa Theologiae III q.46 a.2 ad 3; a.3; q.48 a.2.

claims.claim: Trent taught that Christ merited justification and made satisfaction to the Father (1547) and that the Mass makes present the sacrifice of the cross (1562).
claims.source: Council of Trent, Session 6 ch. 7; Session 22.

claims.claim: Luther called Romans 3:21–26 the centre of the epistle and of the whole Bible.
claims.source: Luther's gloss on Romans 3:23ff in his German Bible (1522 onward).

claims.claim: Luther's breakthrough is described in his 1545 Preface to the Latin Writings.
claims.source: Luther, Preface (1545), LW 34.

claims.claim: Luther's 'happy exchange' and the bridal image are in The Freedom of a Christian (1520).
claims.source: Luther, The Freedom of a Christian (1520).

claims.claim: Calvin's Institutes first 1536, final Latin 1559; Beveridge translation 1845.
claims.source: Standard; CCEL file header.

claims.claim: Socinus attacked satisfaction in De Jesu Christo Servatore (1578); Grotius replied in 1617.
claims.source: Standard histories of doctrine.

claims.claim: C. H. Dodd (1935) read hilasterion as expiation; Leon Morris (1955) as propitiation.
claims.source: C. H. Dodd, The Bible and the Greeks; L. Morris, The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross.

claims.claim: PC(USA) hymnal committee (2013) left out 'In Christ Alone' after its authors declined to change a line about God's wrath.
claims.source: M. L. Bringle, 'Debating hymns', Christian Century, 1 May 2013.

claims.claim: Charles Wesley's 'And can it be' (1738): 'Amazing love! How can it be, / That Thou, my God, shouldst die for me?'
claims.source: Wesley's hymn, public domain.

claims.claim: Paine born Thetford 1737 to a Quaker father and Anglican mother; wrote Part I of The Age of Reason in Paris 1793, published 1794; finished hours before arrest.
claims.source: Conway's introduction in Gutenberg #3743; standard biographies.

claims.claim: Kant argued moral guilt is not transferable like a debt.
claims.source: Kant, Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason (1793), Part Two, Section One.

claims.claim: Girard's scapegoat theory; Violence and the Sacred (1972), Things Hidden (1978), I See Satan Fall Like Lightning (1999).
claims.source: Girard's works.

claims.claim: Brown and Parker (1989) used the phrase 'divine child abuse'.
claims.source: J. C. Brown and R. Parker, 'For God So Loved the World?', in Christianity, Patriarchy, and Abuse (1989).

claims.claim: Delores Williams criticised surrogacy as saving in Sisters in the Wilderness (1993).
claims.source: D. Williams (1993).

claims.claim: Steve Chalke described a crude penal substitution as 'cosmic child abuse' (2003).
claims.source: S. Chalke and A. Mann, The Lost Message of Jesus (2003).

claims.claim: Herbert (1593–1633), rector of Bemerton; The Temple published 1633 by Nicholas Ferrar.
claims.source: Standard biographies; CCEL page.

claims.claim: Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected the charge against the Jews of killing Christ.
claims.source: Nostra Aetate 4.

claims.claim: Earliest crucifixion images (c. 420–430) show Christ alive; Isenheim Altarpiece 1512–1516, for the Antonite hospital.
claims.source: Standard art history (Maskell ivory; Santa Sabina doors; Unterlinden Museum).

claims.claim: 'Were You There' first printed in 1899 (Barton, Old Plantation Hymns).
claims.source: Hymnological reference works.

claims.claim: Painting dates and descriptions (Daddi c. 1320/25; Benvenuto probably 1491; Andrea di Bartolo c. 1380/90; Paolo Veneziano c. 1340/45; Signorelli c. 1504/05; Cossa c. 1473/74).
claims.source: NGA open data via tools/journeys/nga.py show; look points only from 'assistivetext'.
